metadata.title: Teacher collaboration networks as a function of type of collaboration and schools’ structural environment

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses a non-ILSA, school-based teacher survey collected in 2019 from 16 German secondary schools, with seven schools excluded due to low response rates in the network questions. The manuscript does not report the use of complex survey sampling weights or replicate-weight procedures (e.g., BRR/jackknife), and the analysis is conducted at the school/teacher network level using exponential random graph models (ERGMs). Because no ILSA microdata weights (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) are referenced, weighting cannot be verified and is treated as not reported. The key preprocessing step is response-rate filtering (threshold of ≥60% for network questions) and dichotomization of collaboration nominations (values 3–5 coded as ties).

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible values (PVs) are not applicable because the dependent variables are teacher collaboration ties in directed networks (and related network statistics) rather than cognitive achievement scores from an ILSA/PV-based assessment. Missing-data handling is not reported because the paper focuses on network construction from survey nominations and does not describe an imputation or deletion rule for item nonresponse beyond excluding schools with low response rates in the network questions. This omission limits reproducibility regarding how partially missing teacher responses within included schools were treated.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Data were collected in 2019 from 16 German secondary schools participating in a project on teacher collaboration and schools’ structural environments. Seven schools were excluded because response rates in the network questions were below 60%, which the authors state is needed for the ERGM type of analysis. The final analyzed networks cover nine schools, each with between 11 and 93 teachers (total N=366 teachers). Collaboration ties were constructed by asking teachers to nominate up to five colleagues and then dichotomizing Likert-type frequency responses: only values 3 (monthly) to 5 (almost daily) were coded as ties, generating a general collaboration network plus two type-specific networks (exchange of materials; mutual classroom observations).

main_findings.dataset_used: TALIS 2018 (not used; school-based teacher survey in 2019, Germany, secondary schools)
main_findings.target_variable: General teacher collaboration tie formation (directed network)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Exponential random graph model (ERGMs): formal role homophily (0.170, p<0.05); formal role alter (−0.261, p<0.001); gender homophily (0.177, p<0.001); subjects homophily (0.166, p<0.001); reciprocity (3.161, p<0.001); transitivity via GWESP (0.579, p<0.001) and GWDSP (−0.191, p<0.001). Effects reported as log-odds ratios.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using the 2019 German secondary-school teacher survey data (nine schools; N=366 teachers) to model general collaboration tie formation, the study leveraged formal role, gender, teaching experience, attitude, and subject homophily to predict directed collaboration ties, finding that formal-role and subject similarity significantly increased tie probability while attitude and experience effects were largely non-significant. The network also showed strong reciprocity and transitivity (GWESP/GWDSP), indicating that collaboration ties are shaped by both dyadic similarity and higher-order network closure processes. This indicates that school policies should not only encourage collaboration opportunities but also consider how role- and subject-based structures and existing connections facilitate collaboration formation, while recognizing that the study is correlational and based on network modeling rather than causal identification.

main_findings.dataset_used: TALIS 2018 (not used; school-based teacher survey in 2019, Germany, secondary schools)
main_findings.target_variable: Exchange of teaching materials tie formation (directed network)
main_findings.performance_metrics: ERGMs for exchange networks: reciprocity (3.93, p<0.001); GWESP (0.69, p<0.001); GWDSP (−0.26, p<0.001). Exogenous effects include gender outgoing ties (−0.30, p<0.01); attitude ego (0.33, p<0.01) and attitude alter (0.19, p<0.05); subjects homophily (0.24, p<0.001).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using the 2019 German secondary-school teacher survey data to model exchange-of-materials tie formation, the study leveraged gender, teaching experience, formal role, attitude, and subject similarity to predict directed exchange ties, finding that reciprocity and transitivity were strong and that attitude significantly increased both offering and receiving of materials. Gender also mattered for outgoing exchange ties (female teachers exchanged less material than male peers), while subject homophily was significant. This indicates that strengthening collaboration climates may particularly benefit low-cost exchange activities by targeting teachers’ attitudes and by designing structures that connect teachers with compatible roles and subjects, though causality cannot be inferred from ERGM estimates.

main_findings.dataset_used: TALIS 2018 (not used; school-based teacher survey in 2019, Germany, secondary schools)
main_findings.target_variable: Mutual classroom observations tie formation (directed network)
main_findings.performance_metrics: ERGMs for observation networks: reciprocity (4.76, p<0.001); GWESP (0.50, not significant); gender outgoing ties (−0.40, p<0.01); gender homophily (0.27, p=0.06); attitude alter (0.33, p=0.05).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using the 2019 German secondary-school teacher survey data to model mutual classroom-observation tie formation, the study leveraged gender, teaching experience, formal role, attitude, and subject similarity to predict directed observation ties, finding that reciprocity was very strong but transitivity (GWESP) was not significant and that individual-attribute effects were comparatively limited. Gender significantly reduced outgoing observation ties for female teachers, while attitude and gender-homophily effects only narrowly approached significance. This indicates that high-cost co-construction activities like classroom observations may depend more on existing mutual relationships and less on dyadic similarity, implying that school leadership should prioritize structural supports (time/coordination) to enable these ties beyond habitual networks.

main_findings.dataset_used: TALIS 2018 (not used; school-based teacher survey in 2019, Germany, secondary schools)
main_findings.target_variable: General teacher collaboration tie formation moderated by schools’ structural environment
main_findings.performance_metrics: ERGMs by structural environment: Basic-level schools show significant reciprocity (2.95, p<0.001) and GWESP (0.50, p<0.001) with significant GWDSP (−0.31, p<0.001), plus multiple significant homophily effects (except attitude and formal role). High-level schools show structural dominance: reciprocity (3.48, p<0.001) and GWESP (0.65, p<0.001) with GWDSP (−0.15, p<0.03), while individual characteristics are largely non-significant.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using the 2019 German secondary-school teacher survey data to model general collaboration tie formation separately for schools with basic versus high collaborative structural environments, the study leveraged structural-environment group membership alongside dyadic attributes (gender, experience, attitude, formal role, subject) to predict collaboration ties, finding that in basic-structure schools both individual homophily and network closure mattered, whereas in high-structure schools network structural effects dominated and individual attributes were largely irrelevant. This indicates that improving school structures (e.g., scheduled time, leadership commitment, teamwork opportunities) can lower the role of teacher-specific characteristics in collaboration formation, supporting policy efforts focused on institutional conditions rather than only individual-level interventions.

data.outcome_summary: This paper analyzes teacher collaboration networks using a 2019 survey from nine German secondary schools (N=366 teachers; after excluding seven schools with network-question response rates below 60%). Collaboration ties were constructed from directed nominations (up to five colleagues) and dichotomized from Likert-type frequency responses (monthly to almost daily coded as ties), producing a general collaboration network plus two type-specific networks: exchange of teaching materials and mutual classroom observations. The authors estimate exponential random graph models (ERGMs) and report log-odds ratio effects with significance tests. Across networks, reciprocity and transitivity (GWESP/GWDSP) are consistently strong for general collaboration and exchange, while classroom observations show strong reciprocity but weaker/non-significant transitivity. The study finds that formal role and subject similarity predict general collaboration, attitude predicts exchange ties, and structural environment moderates whether individual attributes matter. Limitations include small sample size, dichotomization of tie strength, and no causal identification or PV/weighting framework because the data are not ILSA achievement PVs.
